claims.text: Structural and chemical stability from 473 K to 1923 K is governed by the balance between configurational entropy and a temperature-dependent kinetic barrier to atomic diffusion.
High configurational entropy destabilizes chemically ordered arrangements in equimolar HEA nanoparticles.
Sluggish atomic diffusion inhibits the onset of local chemical ordering or clustering.
Activation of diffusion beyond a threshold causes elemental segregation, local ordering, or clustering that compromises stability.
The initial nanoparticles are near-equiatomic, single-phase, chemically homogeneous disordered solid solutions containing at least five metals.
Changing the initial cooling rate from rapid quenching to slow cooling modulates the initial degree of local ordering.
Thermal annealing across 473–1923 K activates temperature-dependent diffusion.
A controlled or inert atmosphere prevents oxidation and other extrinsic chemical reactions from confounding the thermal response.
Activated atomic diffusion produces local chemical ordering or clustering and associated lattice distortions.
At lower temperatures, limited atomic mobility kinetically stabilizes the disordered solid solution.
Increasing temperature enhances atomic mobility sufficiently to nucleate locally ordered or clustered regions.
Competition between the thermodynamic driving force for ordering or clustering and entropy-stabilized mixing determines stability.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion during subsequent operation or annealing.
Nanoparticles with suppressed diffusion remain uniform disordered solid solutions throughout 473–1923 K.
Retention of a uniform disordered solid solution preserves catalytic and thermoelectric properties.
Greater atomic mobility causes detectable ordering or clustering at higher temperatures.
Ordering or clustering causes catalytic activity or thermoelectric performance to deviate from its baseline.
The prediction requires sufficiently similar atomic sizes and diffusion kinetics for the high-entropy effect to dominate.
Significant atomic-size mismatch or composition changes can alter lattice ordering and phase stability.
The onset temperature and timescale for clustering depend on elemental combination, nanoparticle size, and processing history.

contradictions.description: The initial state and baseline describe uniformly disordered nanoparticles, while the controlled groups are required to differ in initial ordering or clustering and the slow-cooled group is expressly intended to contain some ordering.

Cooling rate is introduced as a way to alter initial ordering, but the prediction later treats rapid quenching as if it inherently suppresses atomic diffusion during subsequent annealing. Initial order and annealing-stage diffusivity are distinct variables.
